lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Polydeuces — I have a commission for you. When you go back up tomorrow — that's your arrangement, isn't it, a day above ground — find me a man called Menippus. The Dog. You'll most likely catch him in Corinth, around the Craneum, or hanging around the Lyceum laughing at the philosophers arguing with each other. Tell him: Diogenes says, if you've had your fill of mocking things up above, come down here — there's considerably more to laugh at. Up there your laughter was always slightly provisional, what with the nagging question of what actually happens after you die. Down here, you'll laugh without interruption, without any reservations, just as I'm doing now. Especially when you see the rich men and the satraps and the tyrants — so diminished, so anonymous — recognisable only by their whimpering, and still going on about how soft and wretched everything is compared to up there.
lines.note: Diogenes delivers this as a list of instructions, not a speech. Dry and practical throughout, as if dictating a memo.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell him that. And also: pack the satchel before he comes. Plenty of lupine beans. And if he passes a crossroads and spots one of Hecate's suppers laid out, or a purification egg, or anything of that sort — he should bring it along.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: I'll pass it on, Diogenes. But so I can actually find him — what does he look like?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Old. Bald. Cloak with more holes than fabric — open to every wind, patched into a kind of patchwork. Always laughing. Mostly at those pompous philosophers.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Easy enough to spot from that description.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: While you're at it — shall I give you something to tell those philosophers as well?

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Go on. It's no great burden.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: On the whole: stop. Stop the babbling, stop the endless wrangling about the nature of everything, stop sprouting horns at each other, manufacturing crocodiles, teaching people to tie their minds in knots with questions that have no answers.
lines.note: References to Stoic logical puzzles — the 'horned' syllogism ('you have what you haven't lost; you haven't lost horns; therefore you have horns') and the 'crocodile' dilemma. Diogenes delivers these as a bored inventory of nonsense.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: They'll say I'm an ignorant barbarian for criticising their wisdom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell them to go to hell. On my behalf.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: That too I will convey, Diogenes.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the rich — dearest Polydeuces, my little Spartan — give them this from me: Why, you fools, are you hoarding gold? Why are you torturing yourselves tallying up interest rates and stacking talent on talent, when you'll be arriving here shortly with one obol to your name?

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: That will be said to them as well.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the beautiful people, the strong ones — Megillus of Corinth, and Damoxenus the wrestler — tell them: down here, there is no golden hair. No bright eyes, no dark eyes. No flush in the cheek. No taut sinew, no broad shoulder. Just dust, as they say. Skulls. Bare of all their beauty.
lines.note: Diogenes lists physical attributes flatly, like a customs officer listing confiscated goods.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: That won't be hard to say to the beautiful and the strong.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the poor — there are plenty who resent their lot and weep over their poverty — tell them: don't cry, don't wail. Explain to them how things stand down here. Equal honours for everyone. They'll see that the rich men they envied aren't any better off than they are. [pause] Oh, and while you're at it — your Spartans. Give them a word from me. Tell them they've gone soft.
lines.note: 'Your Spartans' — a light dig at Polydeuces' Spartan identity. Diogenes saves the most sensitive message for last, almost as an afterthought.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Not a word about Sparta, Diogenes. That I will not carry. Everything else — yes. But not that.
lines.note: Polydeuces is cooperative throughout but draws one clean line. No heat, no drama — just a quiet refusal.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Fine. We'll leave them out of it. Deliver the rest.
